summary: Modular monolith: Phaser (HTML5 game framework), Nakama (Go game backend), PostgreSQL (managed or self-hosted) database on Fly.io. It matches the team's languages and is estimated at $1,600-$3,300 per month.

architecture.name: modular monolith
architecture.justification: One deployable with clear internal modules per feature area suits a team of 5 and 3 feature areas (payments, realtime, file storage): simple to run now, with seams to split later if load demands it.

alternatives.why_not: Adds service boundaries, network calls and per-service deployment that this team does not need at this scale (team 5).
With 3 feature areas, code without module boundaries tends to tangle as the team grows.
Per-request functions suit light, spiky work; this backend runs as a long-lived service on Fly.io, which suits websockets, background jobs and steady traffic better.

frontend.justification: Phaser (HTML5 game framework) matches the team's typescript skills; covers web and android and ios from one codebase; WebGL with canvas fallback; fine for 2D and casual games, below native engines; is a proven choice for gaming projects.

alternatives.why_not: React Native (Expo) scores 10.9 points lower overall, mainly on a game engine client (12.0 points) and fit to this kind of project (0.7 points).
Flutter scores 12.4 points lower overall, mainly on a game engine client (12.0 points) and team skill fit (1.3 points).

tradeoffs: Mobile store builds go through a wrapper such as Capacitor
2D only

backend.justification: Nakama (Go game backend) matches the team's typescript skills; handles many concurrent realtime connections well; go core with a realtime socket API; is a proven choice for gaming projects.

alternatives.why_not: Colyseus (Node.js game server) scores 4.3 points lower overall, mainly on headroom for the expected load (3.3 points) and performance (0.9 points).
Go (net/http + chi) scores 7.8 points lower overall, mainly on a purpose-built game server (8.0 points) and team skill fit (1.4 points).

tradeoffs: Another service to operate
Needs CockroachDB or PostgreSQL

database.justification: PostgreSQL gives ACID transactions for money-handling data; can be placed in Frankfurt (fra), an EU region, which keeps GDPR transfers simple; excellent query planner, rich indexing. It runs as Fly.io Managed Postgres, the managed service on the same cloud as the application, so backups, patching and failover are the provider's job.

alternatives.why_not: CockroachDB scores 2.4 points lower overall, mainly on compliance attestations (1.5 points) and performance (0.8 points).
Neon (serverless Postgres) scores 4.9 points lower overall, mainly on headroom for the expected load (3.3 points) and performance (1.3 points).

tradeoffs: Write scaling beyond one primary needs design

hosting.justification: Fly.io can be placed in Frankfurt (fra), an EU region, which keeps GDPR transfers simple; offers a 99.95% SLA, in line with the 99.9% target; anycast, close to users; is a proven choice for gaming projects.

alternatives.why_not: Google Cloud Run scores 0.56 points higher, which is inside the near-tie range, and loses the tie-break: lower cost first, then complexity and operations load.
Azure Container Apps scores 0.4 points lower overall, mainly on performance (0.5 points).

tradeoffs: Reliability history less steady than hyperscalers

assumptions: Load estimate: peak about 900 requests/second and about 290M requests/month from 120K users in 12 months.
Usage-priced items are shown as a band (0.75x to 1.3x of the estimate) because load figures are order-of-magnitude.
Public list prices of each product, in USD, without taxes, committed-use discounts or developer time.
The 99.9% availability target doubles or adds redundancy for hosting and database where needed.

warnings.message: Use a hosted checkout from a PCI DSS certified provider so card data never reaches your servers.

GDPR: keep a record of processing, sign a data processing agreement with every vendor that handles personal data, support access and erasure requests, and use standard contractual clauses for any transfer outside the EU/EEA; consider EU data residency to keep transfers simple.

A p95 of 100 ms with live updates for users spread across regions is reachable only over persistent connections (WebSockets) to servers in the users' region; avoid cold-starting functions on the hot path and load-test the fan-out at the expected 9,000 concurrent users.

Expected cost ($1,600-$3,300) is inside the $2,500 budget at typical load but can pass it at peak usage; watch hosting (Fly.io, $740-$1,700) and database (PostgreSQL (managed or self-hosted), $810-$1,500) first.

Coins and other digital items sold inside the iOS/Android app must normally go through Apple In-App Purchase and Google Play Billing, which take a 15-30% commission; card checkout (Stripe) stays for the web build and for regions whose rules allow outside payment links.

assumptions: No extra inputs supplied; neutral defaults are used (learning appetite medium, lock-in tolerance medium, budget strictness firm, no hiring plan, no mobile preference).
No compatible stack fits the $2,500 budget, so cost was compared against a reference of about $3,200 per month (the cheapest compatible stack plus 25%) to keep the cheaper options ahead.
Cache: Managed Redis/Valkey (ElastiCache, Memorystore, Azure Cache) replaced by Upstash Redis to bring the stack toward the budget (about $66 per month cheaper).
Queue: NATS JetStream replaced by Google Pub/Sub to bring the stack toward the budget (about $31 per month cheaper).

pipeline: filter each layer by hard constraints

robustness.summary: The same stack wins in 12 of 14 checks. It switches to Google Cloud Run (hosting) when performance counted half as much, maintainability counted twice as much. The runner-up scores 0.56 points higher but costs more, and stacks within 0.75 points count as a tie that the cheaper one wins.

time to market counted half as much

trade_off_options.gains: about 32% cheaper on the core layers plus required supporting services ($1,000-$2,300 against $1,600-$3,300 per month)
gives_up: headroom for the expected load (-3.3 pts)
trade_off_options.summary: Backend Nakama (Go game backend) -> Colyseus (Node.js game server); database PostgreSQL (managed or self-hosted) -> Neon (serverless Postgres): about 32% cheaper on the core layers plus required supporting services ($1,000-$2,300 against $1,600-$3,300 per month). Gives up 5.5 points, mainly on headroom for the expected load (-3.3 pts), scalability (-1.1 pts), performance (-0.8 pts).

trade_off_options.title: More headroom to scale
trade_off_options.summary: Frontend Phaser (HTML5 game framework) -> Unity; database PostgreSQL (managed or self-hosted) -> CockroachDB; hosting Fly.io -> Google Cloud Run: scalability 8.8 instead of 8.0. Gives up 3.2 points, mainly on compliance attestations (-1.5 pts), team skill fit (-1.3 pts), cost (-0.6 pts).

trade_off_options.title: Ship sooner
trade_off_options.summary: Backend Nakama (Go game backend) -> Firebase (BaaS); database PostgreSQL (managed or self-hosted) -> Cloud Firestore; hosting Fly.io -> Cloudflare Pages: time to market 9.2 instead of 7.9. Gives up 9.4 points, mainly on a purpose-built game server (-8.0 pts), vendor lock-in (-3.9 pts), data-model fit (-1.5 pts).
